questions.question: A coherence protocol gives a cache four line states — Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid — so that a line held cleanly by only one core can be written without first broadcasting an invalidation. Which protocol is this?
questions.explanation: MESI's Exclusive state marks a sole, memory-clean copy, so a write to it upgrades to Modified silently; that quiet E->M transition is what distinguishes MESI from MSI.

questions.question: Under MESI, a core reads a line that no other cache holds; because its copy is clean and sole, it may later write the line without any bus transaction. Which state marks this sole clean copy?
questions.explanation: Exclusive means 'only this cache has it, and it still matches memory,' permitting a silent upgrade to Modified on write — the MESI optimization over MSI.

questions.question: A profiler shows that stores hitting L1 update only the cached line and set a per-line flag; DRAM sees the modified data only when that line is later evicted. Which write policy is in use?
questions.explanation: Write-back defers memory updates: the dirty bit marks modified lines, and memory is written only on eviction — minimizing bandwidth versus write-through.

questions.question: A direct-mapped L1 keeps missing because two hot lines share one index. Designers add a tiny fully-associative buffer that holds the line just evicted, so it can be recovered in a cycle or two instead of going to L2. What is this buffer?
questions.explanation: Jouppi's victim cache catches recently evicted lines in a small fully-associative buffer, absorbing conflict misses caused by low associativity.

questions.question: A stride detector notices misses at addresses A, A+64, A+128 and issues line fills for A+192 and A+256 before the core requests them, lifting the hit rate. What technique is at work?
questions.explanation: A hardware stride prefetcher learns regular access patterns and fills lines ahead of demand, hiding miss latency when the prediction is right.

questions.question: Without help, every load would force a four-level page-table walk — four extra memory reads per access. A small associative cache of recent VPN-to-PFN mappings cuts that to about a cycle on a hit. What is this structure?
questions.explanation: The TLB caches page-table entries so virtual-to-physical translation is fast on a hit; a miss still costs a full page-walk or a software refill.

questions.question: A cache maps each address to a single indexed set but lets the block occupy any of that set's 4 ways — a compromise between a rigid direct-mapped cache and an expensive fully-associative one. What organization is this?
questions.explanation: An n-way set-associative cache hashes the address to one set, then searches the n ways in parallel — trading a little hardware for far fewer conflict misses.

questions.question: A loop streams an 8 MB file through a 256 KB L2 exactly once, evicting the loop's real working set for data it will never touch again — and the hit rate collapses. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: Cache pollution is filling the cache with single-use data that displaces reusable lines; non-temporal streaming loads/stores exist to bypass the cache and avoid it.

questions.question: In a write-back cache, a per-line flag is consulted at eviction time to decide whether the line must be copied to DRAM or can simply be dropped. What is this flag called?
questions.explanation: A set dirty bit means the line diverged from memory after a write hit; on eviction a dirty line must be written back, a clean one discarded.

questions.question: An OS keeps a process's page-fault rate low by guaranteeing it frames covering all pages it referenced in the last time window; grant fewer and the process thrashes. What is this set of actively referenced pages?
questions.explanation: Denning's working set is the pages a process referenced in its recent window; allocating below it forces thrashing — paging faster than computing.

questions.question: A cache has a hit time of 2 cycles and a miss penalty of 100 cycles. With a 95% hit rate, what is the AMAT in cycles?
questions.explanation: AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty = 2 + (0.05 x 100) = 2 + 5 = 7 cycles.

questions.question: A direct-mapped cache has 256 blocks with a block size of 32 bytes in a 32-bit address space. How many bits are used for the tag field?
questions.explanation: Block offset = log2(32) = 5 bits; index = log2(256) = 8 bits; tag = 32 - 8 - 5 = 19 bits.

questions.question: A 16 KB cache uses 64-byte blocks. How many cache lines (blocks) does it contain?
questions.explanation: Number of lines = cache size / block size = 16,384 bytes / 64 bytes = 256 cache lines.

questions.question: In a virtual memory system, main memory access takes 100 ns, a page fault takes 10 ms to service, and faults occur once per 10,000 accesses. What is the approximate effective access time?
questions.explanation: EAT = 100 ns + (1/10,000 x 10 ms) = 100 ns + 1,000 ns = 1,100 ns = 1.1 microseconds.

questions.question: A fully associative cache with LRU replacement still misses because a program cycles through more distinct blocks than the cache can hold. Which of the 3 Cs does this describe?
questions.explanation: Capacity misses occur when the working set exceeds the total cache size, so blocks are evicted even though the cache is fully associative.

questions.question: A cache has a 1 ns hit time, a 4% miss rate, and a 100 ns miss penalty. What is the average memory access time (AMAT)?
questions.explanation: AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty = 1 + 0.04 x 100 = 5 ns.

questions.question: L1 has a 1-cycle hit time and 5% miss rate; on a miss, L2 takes 10 cycles, and 20% of L2 accesses miss to DRAM at a 100-cycle penalty. What is AMAT?
A 64 KB direct-mapped cache with 64-byte lines is addressed by 32-bit addresses. How many tag bits does each cache line require?
questions.explanation: Offset = log2(64) = 6 bits; index = log2(64 KB / 64 B) = log2(1024) = 10 bits; tag = 32 - 10 - 6 = 16 bits.

questions.question: In a direct-mapped cache with 16 sets and 64-byte blocks, byte address 1024 (0x400) maps to which set?
questions.explanation: Block number = 1024 / 64 = 16; set = 16 mod 16 = 0.

questions.question: The very first access to a memory block always misses because the block has never been loaded. Which of the three C's is this?
questions.explanation: Compulsory (cold) misses occur on first access and cannot be removed by bigger caches or higher associativity, only by prefetching.
